new.title: Quadratic Equations
sample: Kept short on purpose. In the sample, quadratic comparison appeared in four IBPS Clerk papers (2018 twice, 2019, Dec 2020) with 20 questions, and in none of the 2021 to 2025 Clerk papers or the 12 sister papers of 2025-26.
revision: **Roots:** two numbers that multiply to c (or a x c) and add to b; flip their signs.
**Compare:** all x above all y: x > y; shared root: x ≥ y; interleaved or equal single values: no relation.
**Traps.** x² = k has two roots. √ means the positive root only. x = y exactly is marked "x = y or no relation".

intro: Two equations are given, one in x and one in y. Solve both, then compare every x root with every y root.
There are four short lessons; the sign rule in the first often settles the answer without solving.
What the papers ask: 20 such questions in four IBPS Clerk papers from 2018 to 2020, and none in the 2021 to 2025 Clerk papers or the 2025-26 sister papers checked. So this topic is kept short.
after: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the sign rule and the comparison table.

lessons.title: Roots from a factor pair, and the sign rule
lessons.plain: The starting point: x² + bx + c = 0 is solved by two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Their signs can be read before you solve.
teach: For x² - 13x + 42 = 0, find two numbers that **multiply to 42 and add to 13**: 6 and 7. The roots are x = 6 and x = 7 (the signs flip).
**The sign rule** tells you where the roots lie before any working:
| Middle sign | Last sign | Roots |
| - | + | both positive |
| + | + | both negative |
| either | - | one positive, one negative |
Often this alone decides the comparison: if both x roots are negative and both y roots positive, x < y with no more work.
Checked papers: quadratic comparison was in four IBPS Clerk papers (2018 twice, 2019, Dec 2020) and in none of the 2021 to 2025 Clerk papers or the 2025-26 sister papers checked.

steps: Sign rule: x has + and +, so both roots negative; y has - and +, so both positive.
So every x is below every y: x < y. (The roots are -4, -5 and 3, 4.)

check.q: What are the roots of x² - 11x + 30 = 0?
check.why: 5 x 6 = 30 and 5 + 6 = 11; the middle sign is minus and the last plus, so both roots are positive: 5 and 6.

lessons.title: Comparing the roots
lessons.plain: New: reading the five answer choices correctly.
teach: Put all four roots on one line. Then:
| What you see | Answer |
| every x right of every y | x > y |
| every x right of or on every y (one root shared) | x ≥ y |
| every x left of every y | x < y |
| every x left of or on every y (one root shared) | x ≤ y |
| the roots interleave, or x = y exactly | x = y or no relation |
Watch the last row: when x and y are both a single equal number, the papers mark **"x = y or no relation"**, not x ≥ y.

steps: Every x is at least every y, and 5 is shared: x ≥ y.

check.q: x = 3 or 6, and y = 4 or 5. What is the relation?
check.why: 3 is below both y values but 6 is above both: the roots interleave, so no relation.

lessons.title: When x² has a number in front
lessons.plain: New: 2x² - 7x + 6 = 0. Split the middle number using the product of the first and last.
teach: For ax² + bx + c = 0, find two numbers that **multiply to a x c and add to b**, then divide each by a for the roots (and flip the signs).
2x² - 7x + 6: a x c = 12; 3 and 4 add to 7. Roots 3/2 and 4/2 = 1.5 and 2 (both positive by the sign rule).
The sign rule still works, and fractions compare easily as decimals.

steps: x: 12 = 3 x 4, roots 1.5 and 2. y: 2 and 4.
Every x is at most every y, and 2 is shared: x ≤ y.

check.why: a x c = 24; 6 and 4 add to 10; roots 6/3 = 2 and 4/3, both positive.

tags: Both sides have a leading number.
A real paper, large and small.

lessons.title: Squares, cubes, roots and straight-line pairs
lessons.plain: New: four forms that are not the usual three-term equation.
teach: | Form | Roots | Note |
| x² = 144 | 12 or -12 | a square has two roots |
| y³ = 1728 | 12 only | a cube has one real root |
| x = √625 | 25 only | the √ sign means the positive root |
| two straight-line equations in x and y | solve them together | one x and one y |
The x² = k trap is the usual mistake: forgetting -12 turns "no relation" into "x ≥ y".

steps: Every x is at most y, and 12 is shared: x ≤ y.

check.q: I. x² = 49  II. y = 7. What is the relation?
check.why: x is 7 or -7, both at most 7, with 7 shared: x ≤ y.
